digest.intro: Nuclear satellites, collapsed climate talks, and a trackpad that speaks.

items.title: Russia's Nuclear Anti-Satellite Weapon Could Launch by December
items.source: Kyiv Post / WDR, NDR, Süddeutsche Zeitung
items.blurb: A joint German intelligence investigation reports that Sputnik-S — a fully constructed nuclear-armed satellite — has been stored near Moscow for years and could reach orbit within 60 days, per NATO-circulated warnings from early November. Germany's military space command has briefed Defense Minister Boris Pistorius directly. A single detonation at altitude would fry satellites across multiple orbital shells via EMP — not a targeted kill but a scorched-sky move against the entire ecosystem.

items.title: COP31 Ends Without Agreement — First Failure Since 2009
items.blurb: For the first time in 17 years, a COP ended without a cover decision — the consensus statement that signals global solidarity. The final draft contained no mention of coal, oil, or gas; Saudi Arabia and Russia held the line while the EU, Pacific Island states, and Latin American countries refused to sign. The wreckage in Antalya includes a workers' transition fund and an adaptation assessment plan, but nothing on the core emissions question.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz Attacks Escalate; Ukraine Sinks Russian Warship in Libya
items.blurb: Three more ships struck this weekend in the highest pace of Hormuz attacks since the February U.S.-Iran war began; Iran's IRGC launched simultaneous missile and drone assaults on U.S. positions in Bahrain while Tehran vows to use "all available means" against the naval blockade. Meanwhile, Ukraine struck a Russian warship operating in Libya — the war has now physically reached the Mediterranean.

items.title: Thomas Nagel Isn't Buying Anthropic's Consciousness Argument
items.blurb: In its IPO filing last week, Anthropic listed AI consciousness as a material risk factor — arguing that as models grow more capable, their potential moral status might require costly protective restrictions competitors won't share. Thomas Nagel, the philosopher who wrote the foundational "What is it like to be a bat?" paper on subjective experience, is unconvinced: the gap between functional sophistication and genuine phenomenal consciousness is exactly what makes the question hard, and Anthropic's framing elides it. The story underneath is capital: the company is simultaneously warning investors about consciousness costs and implying those costs are worth bearing — a move that is philosophically interesting and financially strange.

items.title: An AI Model Formally Proved VP ≠ VNP Over Every Field
items.blurb: Anthropic's internal research Claude model discovered and wrote a proof that VP is a proper subset of VNP over every field — the algebraic complexity analog of P≠NP — and formalized it in Lean 4, verified by two independent proof kernels. No human mathematician has checked the underlying paper; the repo explicitly states this and invites scrutiny. If it holds, it's a landmark in both algebraic complexity theory and in what AI systems can contribute to pure mathematics.

items.title: Ladybird Browser Is Now in Alpha
items.blurb: Ladybird ships with its own HTML parser, CSS engine, JavaScript engine, and WebAssembly runtime — not a fork of anything, built from scratch, no corporate parent. It's crashing and incomplete in the way alphas are, but it supports WebDriver and the Firefox DevTools protocol, which means you can already run automated tests and start poking at how a genuinely new engine interprets your WebGL pages. The team is explicitly inviting security researchers to pwn it, treating early exploitation as part of hardening.

items.title: Japanese Metabolism as Bio-City: The Promised Tokyo
items.blurb: Sabukaru's essay on the Metabolism movement traces how Kikutake, Kurokawa, Maki, and Kawazoe — all students of Kenzo Tange — reimagined the city as a living organism after postwar Japan's mass migration and reconstruction shock. The key insight is linguistic: the Japanese word they chose, shinchintaisha (新陳代謝), carries both a biological meaning (cellular exchange) and a Buddhist one (impermanence, renewal), so the architecture was always also theology. Ocean city proposals, plug-in capsule towers, interchangeable infrastructure — this is where cyberpunk urbanism and Buddhist impermanence actually met.

items.title: The Worst Possible Swing Technique
items.blurb: Steve Mould built a robot specifically to pump a playground swing in the least efficient way possible, then used it to demonstrate pumping resonance — the physics of how energy couples into an oscillating system at the wrong phase. It's a maker project that becomes a physics lecture without announcing itself as one, which is exactly Mould's signature move.

items.title: No Speaker — Your MacBook Trackpad Can Talk
items.blurb: The Force Touch trackpad contains a haptic motor designed to simulate a click — NO SPEAKER drives it at up to 4,000 cycles per second, fast enough to produce audible sound, and uses it to synthesize speech, song, and instrument-like tones. One curl command, no speakers required; the whole trick exploits the fact that the motor is fundamentally a small linear actuator with enough bandwidth to carry audio frequencies. It's a beautiful piece of constraint-led hardware invention that makes you hear your laptop differently.

facts.fact: Russia's Sputnik-S nuclear satellite has reportedly been fully constructed and stored near Moscow for several years — it was not recently built in response to current tensions.

Anthropic listed AI consciousness as a formal material risk factor in its IPO filing, acknowledging that taking model sentience seriously could impose costs on the company that competitors won't bear.
The MacBook Force Touch trackpad's haptic motor can be driven at 4,000 Hz — well within the range of human hearing — turning it into a functional audio transducer without any speaker.

People with Type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer's at a rate of roughly 4.7 per 1,000 patients per year, and face a 53% higher adjusted relative risk compared to those without diabetes, per a meta-analysis of 40 studies.
The Lean 4 formalization of the VP ≠ VNP proof was written entirely by AI models, and the repository explicitly states that no human mathematician has verified the underlying paper.

make_something.prompt: The Metabolist architects treated the city as a living organism with replaceable cellular units — capsules that plug in and out of permanent infrastructure. Take one fixed object in your space (a shelf, a wall panel, a desk surface) and redesign it as a Metabolist 'exchange unit': what's the permanent spine it plugs into, and what's the temporary cell that gets swapped out? Sketch or prototype the attachment logic — the joint is the whole idea.

art_picks.title: Jeanne Dielman, 23 quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles
art_picks.creator: Chantal Akerman
art_picks.why: A three-and-a-half-hour real-time portrait of domestic ritual as feedback loop — Akerman turns repetition into a system so precise that the tiniest deviation becomes devastating. The film is about invisible structure made visible through obsessive craft, which is exactly what you make.

art_picks.title: Mycelium Studies / Drift Series
art_picks.creator: Roxy Paine
art_picks.why: Paine's large-scale stainless-steel dendrite and mycelium sculptures are generative 3D systems made physical — branching algorithms you can walk under. His obsessive replication of natural growth logic into inert metal is the physical/digital boundary pushed into sculpture.

art_picks.title: Selected Ambient Works Volume II
art_picks.creator: Aphex Twin
art_picks.why: Eighteen tracks with no titles, only images — Aphex stripped music to pure system and texture, forcing the listener's brain to construct narrative from almost nothing. It's about how minds build reality from minimal signal, and it still sounds like nothing else made before or since.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: A neural network trained on fMRI brain scans generates hallucinatory images on freestanding screens, mutated in real time by visitors' gazes and simulated cancer-cell data — the closing week of the most rigorous AI-perception show NYC has seen, and the exact edge where machine cognition and human presence collide.

events.name: Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses
events.why: 140 haute couture pieces organized around eleven chapters — mathematics, neuroscience, marine biology, paleontology — with fossils from the AMNH beside dresses grown from bioengineering and 3D printing; this is fashion functioning as systems theory, closing in two weeks.

events.name: James Turrell: Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue
events.venue: Almine Rech New York, 361 Broadway, Manhattan
events.why: Over fifteen works including a new Shallow Space and new Glassworks — Turrell's entire project is about how the brain constructs reality from light, which maps directly onto the perceptual and systems questions you're circling in your own work.

events.name: Kehinde Wiley: What the Light Becomes
events.why: Wiley's return to New York as subject — conceived as a love letter to the city that launched his practice — with the work explicitly interrogating how identity, status, and symbol operate through portraiture and public space, which is a live demonstration of his interest in how symbols and power circulate.

events.name: LCD Soundsystem NYC Residency — Brooklyn Steel Run (100th Show + Beyond)
events.why: Four consecutive nights anchored by the band's 100th annual residency show — James Murphy's project has always been music about music culture, downtown identity, and time passing, performed with a precision that makes the room feel like a feedback loop between crowd and system.
